subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the intervals on which f(x) = x² − 3x + 8 is increasing or decreasing.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what inequality you solve for increasing and what you solve for decreasing, and say whether a second derivative is needed.

steps.label: Differentiate
steps.margin_note: First mark. State that f is a polynomial and so is differentiable everywhere — that is what lets the sign of f′ decide the behaviour on the whole real line.
lines: f is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable for every real x.
The sign of f′ decides where f increases and where it decreases:
f is increasing where f′(x) > 0, and decreasing where f′(x) < 0.

recall.must_convey: That f′(x) = 2x − 3, and that the sign of f′ decides increasing and decreasing.
accept: differentiate to get two x minus three
the sign of the first derivative decides it
derivative sign chusi increasing decreasing cheptam
f is a polynomial so it is differentiable everywhere

steps.why: The first derivative measures the rate of change. Where it is positive the values rise as x rises, and where it is negative they fall, so its sign is the whole answer to this question.
common_mistakes: Carrying the constant 8 into the derivative.
steps.memory_tip: Increasing and decreasing are questions about the FIRST derivative's sign. Maximum and minimum are questions about where it is zero.

steps.label: Solve f′(x) > 0 and f′(x) < 0
steps.margin_note: Two marks, one for each inequality. Solve them as inequalities, not by testing a couple of sample numbers — the examiner looks for the two lines of algebra.
lines: At x = 3/2 the derivative is zero, so f is neither increasing nor decreasing at that single point.

recall.must_convey: That 2x − 3 > 0 gives x > 3/2 and 2x − 3 < 0 gives x < 3/2.
accept: solve two x minus three greater than zero
x greater than three by two for increasing
x less than three by two for decreasing
the turning value is three by two
at three by two the derivative is zero

steps.why: The derivative here is linear, so it changes sign exactly once. Solving the two inequalities gives both intervals directly and shows the boundary value 3/2 in the same working.
common_mistakes: Dividing by 2 and writing x > 3 instead of x > 3/2.
Reversing the inequality sign when dividing by the positive number 2.
steps.memory_tip: Set the derivative to zero once to find the boundary, then decide which side is positive. A linear derivative changes sign only at that single value.

steps.label: State the two intervals
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Write both intervals in interval notation and name which is which. No second derivative is needed anywhere in this question.
lines: The boundary value 3/2 belongs to neither open interval, since f′(3/2) = 0.
The values fall up to x = 3/2 and rise after it, which matches the intervals found.

lines.text: ∴ f is decreasing on (−∞, 3/2) and increasing on (3/2, ∞)

recall.must_convey: That f is decreasing on (−∞, 3/2) and increasing on (3/2, ∞).
accept: decreasing on minus infinity to three by two
increasing on three by two to infinity
the function falls first and then rises
three by two varaku decreasing, taruvatha increasing
write both intervals in interval notation
no second derivative is needed for this question

steps.why: The question asks for intervals, so the answer is two intervals with their labels, not a single value of x. The check with three sample values confirms the direction of each one.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two labels and calling the left interval increasing.
Applying the second derivative test, which answers a different question.
steps.memory_tip: For an upward parabola the graph falls to the vertex and rises after it, so decreasing always comes first and increasing second.
